## Chapter IV.

COAL COUNTRIES, AND THE QUANTITIES OF COAL PRODUCED IN GREAT BRITAIN, BELGIUM, FRANCE, PRUSSIA, SAXONY, AUSTRIA, SPAIN, AUSTRALIA, THE UNITED STATES, ETC. — AMOUNT OF DUTY, NUMBER OF COLLIERIES, WORKMEN, ETC. VARIETIES OF COAL — HOUSEHOLD, STEAM, (ADMIRALTY REPORT), COKING, GAS, SPLINT, CANNEL, AND OTHER VARIETIES. DURATION OF THE COAL FIELDS.

Coal Countries and their Products.

GREAT BRITAIN. — Great Britain, it is almost needless to repeat, ranks first in the quantity and quality of its Coal, as compared with other Coal-producing countries; yet as regards the Coal-fields of the World, the United States possesses by far the greatest area of Coal formation, whilst British America alone exceeds that of Great Britain, France, Belgium, and Spain united. In England we have not, as in many other countries, any official details of the production and distribution of Coal, excepting the coasting trade and foreign exportation; though, since the appointment of Inspectors of Mines in 1850, an approximation of the total produce may be arrived at. Each Inspector, in his Annual Report, generally refers to the quantity of Coal raised in his district ; and these Reports are presented to the House of Commons, and published annually — See article "Government Inspection."

The Coal formation of Great Britain occupies an area of 11,859 square miles; the extraction of Coal in 1856 was 66,645,450 tons, valued at the pit's mouth at £16,663,862, The Coal was raised from 2,946 pits, collieries having generally more than one pit to each. The hewers employed in the pits average 1,000 tons per annum, but including off-hand men, putters, boys, and others employed about a colliery, the quantity of Coal raised averages about 500 tons for each person per annum. For an account of the distribution of the various Coal-fields or beds, see page 8. Descriptions of important individual collieries, amount of capital invested, profit, &c., will appear in following chapters; and in giving a History of the Coal Trade at a further advanced portion of the work, numerous details will be introduced connected with the produce of Coal in the United Kingdom.

BELGIUM. — We learn from official papers published in Brussels, that the earliest reference to mineral Coal in Belgium was in the year 1198 or 1200, in the district of Liege, where tradition gives the credit of the application, as a fuel, to a blacksmith. From this time there seems to be evidence of its being in ordinary use, and that the business of its extraction had, from a remote period, prior to the 15th century, been subject to the supervision of an especial court or jury.

In Belgium there are three Coal-fields, viz. :— Mons District, in Hainault Province, the average depth of which is 810 feet; Charleroy, Hainault Province, average depth, 482 feet; and L'Esperance Mine, Liege Province, of 1476 maximum feet.

The area of the Belgian Coal formation is estimated at 518 miles. In 1844-5 there were in full operation 212 mines, and 97 others not in work, making in all 309 mines, comprising 540 Coal pits in operation and construction; and employing 38,500 miners and 500 steam engines for various purposes, of an aggregate force of 22,841 horse power. The produce of their labour was 4,445,240 tons, which were returned at the value of £1,660,000 at the place of extraction.

In 1845-6, the quantity of Coal raised was 4,960,077 tons; in 1850, 5,800,000 tons, raised from 408 working pits, by 47,949 operatives, giving an average extraction from each pit of 14,260 tons, and an average individual production, including those employed above and below ground, of 122 tons. In 1852, the yield was 6,250,000 tons. In 1855, the production increased to 8,409,330 tons; the quantity raised in 1856 remaining nearly the same. Of this quantity France was a purchaser in 1856, of 3,119,630 tons. — See next page.

Belgium pays 1s. 6d. per ton duty on all Coal sent to France. In 1855, the home consumption of Coal was 1,194 tons to every 1,000 inhabitants.

The fittings up of the Belgian collieries are said not to be adapted to effect economic working; the shafts not being amply secured for furnace ventilation; and the mode of handling the Coal, when brought to the surface, is attended with unnecessary labour.

FRANCE. — Coal is supposed to have been used in France before the 14th century. It is affirmed with certainty that in the year 1321 Coal was extracted from the mines of Roche-la-Moliere, in the Loire basin. Two centuries after (1520), Coal began to be imported from England in to Paris; and, as was the case in London, a good deal of excitement prevailed as to its effect upon the atmosphere and the health of the inhabitants. The faculty of Medicine were consulted, and they reported that, with proper precautions to avoid the inconvenience arising from the smoke, Coal would not act in any way prejudicially to the public health. Without referring to the imposition of taxes on the importation of Coal, and other state and municipal regulations of former times, we will confine our statements to the consumption and produce of Coal in France within the last few years. The subject is an important one; France ranks next to Great Britain as a Coal-consuming country, and she is the largest Coal-importing country in the world.

The extent of the French Coal formation is estimated at 1,920 square miles; the number of Coal-fields is 64; they comprise 448 mines, varying from 845 to 1,635 feet in depth. By far the largest are those of Loire and Valenciennes, and more than half the annual production of Coal is extracted from thence. At these mines 16,000 hands are employed, at an annual outlay of £410,000, or £25 per man, producing 2,703,980 tons.

About the year 1832, the French Legislature first instituted the system of mine inspection; the most competent mining engineers were engaged, and the result is reported from time to time to be most satisfactory.
